title: Handed down (CCC 74–79)
hook: the apostles handed on their mission to bishops

segments.voice: Yesterday, revelation: God making himself known in stages, Noah, Abraham, Israel, then the Son. Your line was step by step. What did you let take one more step? Today, how it's passed on. Day one thousand sixty-five.

"And the things which thou hast heard of me by many witnesses, the same commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also." That's Paul, writing to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims. Follow the people in that one sentence. Paul speaks. Timothy hears. Timothy hands it to faithful men. They teach others. And the others, presumably, will teach others again. It's a relay, written into a single verse. Today's word is about that relay, and how the Catholic Church understands it: apostolic succession.
screen: `PAUL TO TIMOTHY.` → `TO FAITHFUL MEN.` → `TO OTHERS ALSO.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls this whole process of handing on the faith tradition, a living transmission. It says the apostles handed on what they had received in two ways. By word of mouth: their preaching, their example, the communities and customs they set up. And in writing, in the books that became the New Testament. Then it adds a third thing. To keep the gospel whole and alive in the Church, the apostles left bishops as their successors, handing over to them their own teaching role. That's apostolic succession. Catholic teaching sees today's bishops as successors of the apostles, each one ordained by the laying on of hands by bishops before him. An early letter already speaks this way. A letter from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth, which tradition credits to Clement, says the apostles appointed leaders and then made provision that, when those leaders died, other approved men should succeed to their ministry. Orthodox Christians also hold to the succession of bishops. Other churches understand faithfulness to the apostles in other ways, some by holding to the apostles' teaching in scripture rather than to a line of bishops. Catholic teaching adds a limit. A little further on, the Catechism says the Church's teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it. The bishop is a link in the chain, not the source of what runs through it. That's the carry: an unbroken line. In the Catholic picture it's less a family tree of power than a chain of hands, each one passing on what it was given, and answerable for passing it on whole.
screen: `TRADITION: A LIVING HANDING-ON.` · `IN PREACHING AND IN WRITING.` · `BISHOPS AS THE APOSTLES' SUCCESSORS.` · `A LINK IN THE CHAIN, NOT THE SOURCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your bishop by name, or, if you don't pray, simply hold that person in mind. If you don't know the name, you can look it up after the bell; for now, think of whoever holds that role where you live. Settle, and breathe. Think about the weight of the job: one person asked to keep an old message whole, in a place full of new problems. If you pray, you can say their name and ask God's help for them. If you don't, wish them wisdom, plainly, the way you'd wish it for anyone carrying something heavy. The bell holds the time.
Apostolic succession. The bishops as successors of the apostles, a teaching role handed on hand to hand, in service of the word of God. Today's word.
Your line: an unbroken line. Today, pass on one good thing someone once taught you, a recipe, a skill, a piece of advice, to someone who can carry it further. Day one thousand sixty-five.

howItsDone: At every Mass, the Eucharistic Prayer names the pope and the local bishop, and bishops are ordained by other bishops through the laying on of hands, which Catholics understand as the succession from the apostles.

fork.setup: you're one of the apostles, and you won't live forever. how do you make sure the message outlasts you?
options: trust that people will remember it
preach, write, and provide for successors
write it down and leave it at that
fork.reveal: the Catechism says they preached and wrote, and left bishops as their successors; the letter credited to Clement says they provided for others to succeed.

original.note: Greek: an overseer. The New Testament word that Catholic Bibles render as bishop.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of bishops claiming power.
what it means: Catholic teaching that the apostles left bishops as successors to keep the gospel whole, a role passed on by the laying on of hands.
what a scholar hears: 2 Timothy 2:2's relay of teachers; the Roman letter credited to Clement on approved men succeeding; the Catechism on a teaching office that serves the word of God.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of 2 Timothy 2:2 (the verse begins 'And the things...'; the hook drops 'And').

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): tradition as living transmission CCC 78; preaching and writing CCC 76; bishops as successors 'handing over their own teaching role' CCC 77 (from Dei Verbum 7); the teaching office serves the word of God is CCC 86, just outside the day's range.
1 Clement 42 and 44 paraphrased; the letter is sent in the name of the church of Rome and is credited to Clement by tradition. Confirm the paraphrase.
'Other churches ... some by holding to the apostles' teaching in scripture rather than to a line of bishops': check this is fair. Anglican and some Lutheran claims to succession are left aside.
